spec: Split text on whitespace into words and greedily pack them into lines of at most width characters, separated by single spaces, like a simple word wrap. Unlike a plain wrap, if a single word is longer than width, cut it into consecutive width-character chunks (each chunk its own line) until the remainder fits, then continue packing normally. Empty text returns an empty list.

Greedily word-wrap text to width characters per line as usual. If the result has more than max_lines lines, keep only the first max_lines lines and append '...' to the end of the last kept line, truncating that line first if needed so it still fits within width characters (including the ellipsis).
visible_tests: assert wrap_fixed_lines('one two three four five', 6, 2) == ['one', 'two...']
assert wrap_fixed_lines('a b c d', 3, 2) == ['a b', 'c d']

spec: Treat each line of the input (split on newline characters) as a separate paragraph. Wrap each paragraph independently using greedy word wrap at the given width, keeping an empty paragraph as an empty line. Join the wrapped paragraphs back together with newline characters, preserving the original paragraph order.
visible_tests:
assert wrap_preserve_paragraphs('a b
c d e', 3) == 'a b
c d
e'

spec: Split text on whitespace and greedily pack words into lines of at most width characters (with a single space between words on the same line), exactly like a simple word wrap. Instead of returning the lines, return only the integer number of lines this would produce. Empty or whitespace-only text returns 0.

Remove up to n leading space characters from each line of text (split on newline). If a line has fewer than n leading spaces, remove only the leading spaces it actually has and leave the rest of the line untouched. Rejoin the lines with newline characters.
Split text on newline characters and prepend n copies of the given single character ch to every line, including lines that are empty. Rejoin the lines with newline characters.

Given a list of lines, find the minimum number of leading spaces among all non-blank lines (a blank line is one that is empty or contains only whitespace). Remove that many leading spaces from the start of every line, leaving blank lines unchanged. If there are no non-blank lines, return the list unchanged.
Split text on newline characters. Leave the first line unchanged, but prepend n spaces to every subsequent line, including empty ones. Rejoin the lines with newline characters.

For each line of text (split on newline), if the line begins with a single tab character, replace just that leading tab with four spaces, leaving the rest of the line untouched. Lines that do not start with a tab are returned unchanged.
visible_tests: assert dedent_tabs('no tab here') == 'no tab here'

spec: Given a list of strings, prepend n spaces to each one and join the resulting strings with newline characters into a single string. An empty list of lines produces an empty string.

For every line of text (split on newline) that starts with at least old_n leading space characters, remove the first old_n spaces and put new_n spaces in their place. Lines with fewer than old_n leading spaces are left completely unchanged. Rejoin the lines with newline characters.
visible_tests: assert reindent('    a\n    b', 4, 2) == '  a\n  b'

spec: Given a list of item strings and a bullet marker string, render one line per item as the bullet followed by a space and the item text, joined together with newline characters. An empty list of items produces an empty string.

Given a list of item strings, render one line per item numbered starting at 1, formatted as the number, a period, a space, then the item text. Join all lines with newline characters. An empty list produces an empty string.

Given a list of (level, text) pairs where level is a non-negative integer nesting depth, render one line per pair: two spaces per level of indentation, then a dash, a space, and the text. Join the lines with newline characters. An empty list of items produces an empty string.

Given a list of (text, done) pairs where done is a boolean, render one line per pair: '[x] ' followed by the text if done is True, otherwise '[ ] ' followed by the text. Join the lines with newline characters. An empty list produces an empty string.
visible_tests: assert render_checklist([('buy milk', False), ('clean', True)]) == '[ ] buy milk\n[x] clean'
assert render_checklist([('done task', True)]) == '[x] done task'

spec: Given a list of item strings with at most 26 items, render one line per item labeled with lowercase letters starting at 'a', formatted as the letter, a period, a space, then the item text. Join the lines with newline characters. An empty list produces an empty string.

Given a list of item strings, a bullet marker string, and an indent width, render one line per item as indent spaces, then the bullet, a space, then the item text. Join the lines with newline characters. An empty list of items produces an empty string.

Given a list of item strings, render one line per item numbered starting at 1, where the numbers are zero-padded on the left so they all have the same width as the total number of items (for example, with 12 items the numbers run '01.' through '12.'). Join the lines with newline characters. An empty list produces an empty string.
Given a list of (term, definition) pairs, render one line per pair as the term, a colon, a space, then the definition. Join the lines with newline characters. An empty list produces an empty string.
visible_tests: assert render_definition_list([('cat', 'an animal'), ('run', 'to move fast')]) == 'cat: an animal\nrun: to move fast'

spec: Given a digit string and a count keep, mask every character except the last keep characters, replacing masked characters with '*' and keeping the total length unchanged. If keep is zero or negative, mask the whole string; if keep is greater than or equal to the string's length, return the string unchanged.

Given a digit string, keep the first 3 and last 2 characters visible and replace everything in between with '*' characters, preserving the total length. If the string has 5 or fewer characters, mask the entire string.

Given a phone number string formatted as three dash-separated groups 'AAA-BBB-CCCC', replace the middle group with the same number of asterisk characters and leave the first and last groups unchanged.

Given an international phone number string formatted as '+CC-AAA-BBB-CCCC' (dash-separated segments), keep the leading country-code segment and the final segment unchanged, and replace every segment in between with asterisk characters of the same length as that segment.

Given a digit string and a single mask character ch, replace all but the last 4 characters with ch, keeping the last 4 characters visible and the total length unchanged. If the string has 4 or fewer characters, return it unchanged.

Given a dash-formatted phone number string, optionally followed by a space, the letter 'x', and an extension number (for example '123-456-7890 x123'), mask all digits of the phone number except the last 4 with '*', keeping the dashes in their original positions. Any extension suffix is left fully visible and unchanged; if there is no extension, none is added.

Given a digit string and two counts keep_first and keep_last, keep that many characters visible at the start and end of the string respectively and mask everything in between with '*', preserving the total length. If keep_first plus keep_last is greater than or equal to the string's length, return the string unchanged.

Format a numeric amount as a US dollar string with a leading '$', thousands separated by commas, and exactly two decimal places. Negative amounts are formatted with a leading minus sign before the dollar sign, for example -1234.5 becomes '-$1,234.50'.

Format a numeric amount as a dollar string with thousands separators and two decimal places. Non-negative amounts are formatted as '$X.XX'; negative amounts are formatted with the absolute value in parentheses instead of a minus sign, like '($X.XX)'.

Given an integer number of cents, format it as a dollar string with a leading '$', thousands separators on the dollar part, and exactly two digits for the cents. Negative cent values produce a leading minus sign, for example -5 becomes '-$0.05'.

Format a numeric amount with thousands separators and two decimal places, prefixed by a given currency symbol string. Negative amounts have a minus sign placed before the symbol, for example -1234.5 with symbol '€' becomes '-€1,234.50'.

Format a numeric amount rounded to the nearest whole dollar as a string with a leading '$' and thousands separators, with no decimal point. Negative amounts produce a leading minus sign before the dollar sign.

Given two numeric amounts low and high, format each as a dollar string with thousands separators and two decimal places, and combine them as 'low-high' separated by a hyphen, for example '$10.00-$20.00'.

Format a numeric amount with thousands separators and two decimal places, followed by a space and the given currency code string, for example 1234.5 with code 'USD' becomes '1,234.50 USD'. Negative amounts produce a leading minus sign before the number.

Format a numeric amount as an accounting-style dollar string: zero is always shown as '$0.00', positive amounts are shown as '$X.XX' with thousands separators and two decimal places, and negative amounts are shown the same way but wrapped in parentheses instead of using a minus sign.
Given a fraction, round it to the nearest whole percent and format it as a string with a trailing '%' sign and no decimal point, for example 0.42 becomes '42%'.

Given a numerator and a denominator, compute numerator divided by denominator as a percentage formatted with exactly two decimal places and a trailing '%' sign. If the denominator is zero, return the string 'N/A' instead.

Given a fraction, convert it to a percentage with one decimal place and prefix it with an explicit '+' sign if the value is zero or positive, or a '-' sign if it is negative, for example 0.05 becomes '+5.0%' and -0.05 becomes '-5.0%'.

Given an old value and a new value, compute the percent change from old to new as (new - old) / old times 100, formatted with one decimal place, prefixed by an explicit '+' for a non-negative change or '-' for a negative one, followed by a '%' sign. If old is zero, return the string 'N/A' instead.

Given a fraction, convert it to a percentage rounded to at most two decimal places, but drop any trailing zero digits (and a trailing decimal point if nothing follows it) before appending a '%' sign. For example 0.5 becomes '50%', 0.505 becomes '50.5%', and 0.50051 becomes '50.05%'.

Join a list of strings into a natural-language list using commas, with 'and' before the last item. Zero items produce an empty string, one item is returned as-is, two items are joined as 'A and B', and three or more items are joined with commas and an oxford comma before 'and', like 'A, B, and C'.
